title: TB7-16800

Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Sierra Leone and appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Sierra Leone and appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), denying his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute its own decision that he is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, or, in the alternative, refer his claim back to the RPD for redetermination.
He has presented new evidence to the RAD that he argues establishes that he faces a serious possibility of persecution as a gay man, and/or perceived gay man in Sierra Leone. Determination

The appeal is allowed pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. Role of the RAD

As held by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica,2 the RAD must review RPD decisions on a correctness standard with respect to questions of law and findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), which raise no issue of the credibility of oral evidence. Deference may be required when the RPD is in an advantageous position with respect to the assessment of oral evidence.3 In this appeal, I was able to review and understand the hearing, as well as the record. I do not find that the RPD was in an advantageous position in assessing this evidence, and do not apply a deferential standard. Background

The Appellant alleges that he is gay and has had same sex relationships in Sierra Leone, as well as in Canada. The Appellant came to Canada in XXXX 2014 on a student visa. He made a claim for refugee protection in February 2017. The Appellant had his claim heard by the RPD on July 11, 2017 and was denied in a written decision on July 24, 2017. The determinative issue before the RPD was credibility.

The Appellant's original appeal was dismissed for lack of perfection on January 24, 2018. The appeal was reopened by the RAD in a decision dated September 26, 2018. The Appeal was received by the RAD on November 13, 2018. Appellant's Arguments

The Appellant submits new evidence in his appeal. He does not challenge any of the RPD's findings on credibility. The Appellant argues that the sole issue before the RAD is based upon the new evidence and whether he should be found to be a Convention Refugee or a person in need of protection. Admissibility of the new evidence

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

The second step in the analysis for new evidence is to consider it in relation to the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.4 In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD will apply the Raza factors, minus the "materiality" factor, as this is to be assessed in light of subsection 110(6) only.

The Appellant submits the following four pieces of new evidence that all relate to the publication of his name, photo, and personal circumstances as part of his original Appeallant's Record. * Article from the Concord Times titled "For the love of Gay..." dated April 19, 2018; * Printout of "About Us" section of the Concord Times website; * Screenshots of the above two pages on a computer; and, * Printouts from All Africa and Online Newspapers.com about Concord Times.5

The Appellant submits in his affidavit that accompanied his appeal record, that in May 2018 he was informed by his friend that his name and photograph appeared in a newspaper article referring to him being gay and his family being attacked. The Appellant was able to locate the article in October 2018.

The Appellant submits that this evidence meets both the statutory and jurisprudential tests for admissibility. I agree. The article is dated April 19, 2018 and therefore, was not available, or expected at the time his refugee claim was rejected. The article and evidence related to the publication of the article is relevant and probative, as it directly relates to his claim and personal circumstances. The source is a Sierra Leonian newspaper and is therefore credible. I accept the new evidence and will consider it in the appeal. Rule 29 new evidence

The Appellant also submits new evidence that post-dates his appeal. Under Rule 29 the factors to consider as to whether to allow an application include: the document's relevant and probative value; any new evidence the document brings to the appeal; and whether the Appellant could have provided this as part of the appeal record.

On January 15, 2019, the RAD received further evidence from the Appellant. The new documents include: * Physical copy of the Concord Times newspaper dated April 19, 2018; * Affidavit of XXXX XXXX, sworn on December 10, 2018 and her ID; * Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX, sworn on December 10, 2018 and her ID; * Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX sworn on December 10, 2018 and her ID.6

The Appellant submits that his original new evidence was an online edition of a newspaper article, but that he was attempting to obtain a hard copy of the newspaper. This new evidence is the newspaper version. He also submits affidavits from associates indicating that they have seen the article and his sexual identity is now known in the community.
The Appellant also submits, as part of his Rule 29 application, that he has been attempting to obtain this evidence prior to submitting his appeal record.

I accept that the new evidence is both relevant and probative, and accept the Appellant's explanations with respect to why there was a delay in obtaining these documents. I also find the new evidence meets the statutory and jurisprudential tests (subsection. 110(4) of IRPA and Singh/Raza factors).
I will consider the new evidence in my analysis below. RAD Analysis of the Appeal The Appellant is lacking in credibility with respect to his original claim

The RPD found, and I agree, that the Appellant was lacking in credibility with respect to central aspects of his refugee claim regarding his sexual orientation. For example, his oral testimony regarding how his family in Sierra Leone found out he was gay was inconsistent with his Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative. Having reviewed the RPD hearing, the Appellant's testimony became more and more convoluted. According to his BOC he was outed after encountering his partner's ex-wife at the Yorkdale mall7. She reported it to his brother in Sierra Leone. However, in his oral testimony he recounted a different sequence of events. He was unable to explain the discrepancies. His testimony was also tied to his schooling here in Canada, indicating that his brother was paying for his international student fees, which were stopped after the discovery that he is gay in 2016. However, this too was inconsistent with his written evidence8, which indicated that his schooling ended in 2015, one year before he was outed.

This narrative is also inconsistent with corroborating evidence submitted indicating that the Appellant's sexual orientation was disclosed to his family by a man names "XXXX".9 The Appellant testified that it was not XXXX, but a man named XXXX.

There were other aspects of his refugee claim that were lacking in credibility, including his testimony about his same sex relationships in Sierra Leone and in Canada. Generally, I agree with the findings made by the RPD, its reasoning is correct in my view. The new evidence is determinative

The Appellant bases his appeal only on the introduction of new evidence. He does not challenge any of the RPD's findings. He submits that the new evidence (both evidence that came with his appeal and the rule 29 new evidence) is determinative. I agree with this submission.

I have examined the website of the Concord Times that the Appellant submitted. I have also considered the online article about the Appellant in both content and style. I have a number of credibility concerns related to the content and timing of the article. The article contains no byline, there is no author associated with the article. The Appellant does not explain how his photograph was obtained or why the article is being published fours years after he has left the country, and two years after allegedly being outed. The article is poorly written; it contains grammatical and spelling errors, sentences end abruptly, and do not make sense. There are a number of credibility problems with the article.

However, I accept, based upon the evidence from the Appellant, that the article has been published online and in print form. It remains on the Concord Times website. The article states the following: The Appellant is identified as a gay man; that he resides in Canada; his father has disowned him; his family members have faced violence due to the discovery of the sexual identity of the Appellant. As indicated by the Appellant, I see that the article contains the Appellant's full name and photograph. Other evidence submitted confirms that the Concord Times is a leading newspaper in Sierra Leone, founded in 1992 and based in Freetown. The newspaper is distributed nationwide in Sierra Leone and it is relied on by other news outlets as a source of news.

I accept that the new evidence, despite the credibility concerns identified, establishes that the Appellant faces a serious possibly of persecution in Sierra Leone on account of the perception that he is gay.

The objective evidence refers to a "hostile" socio-political environment for LGBTQ individuals. Discrimination is enshrined in the legislation; Offences against the Person Act 1861. Section 61"Whosoever shall be convicted of the abominable crime of buggery, committed either with mankind or with any animal, shall be liable, at the discretion of the court, to be kept in penal servitude for life or for any term not less than ten years."10

Other evidence found in the National Documentation Package (NDP) indicates that: The constitution does not offer protection from discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. Sexual orientation and gender-identity civil society groups alleged that because the law prohibits male-to-male sexual activity, the law limits lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) persons from exercising the freedoms of expression and peaceful assembly.11

Submissions from the Appellant highlight other aspects of the NDP that address the situation for LGBTQ individuals in Sierra Leone. * The most significant human rights issues included the criminalization of same-sex sexual conduct, leading to the arrest of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex individuals;12 * Members of the LGBT community face discrimination and violence. LGBTI people are often denied medical services, and there are no laws against hate crimes based on sexual orientation;13 * An extensive report in 2013 concluded that "individuals in Sierra Leone are frequently subjected to discrimination and high levels of verbal abuse, violence and harassment by the public officials, members of their communities and even their own families. The combination of discriminatory laws, backed up by ignorance, lack of legal protection, and intolerance.by high rank politicians and religious leaders in public, create an environment where LGBTI individuals cannot feel safe;14 * Sierra Leone rejected recommendations of the UN Human Rights Council to repeal all provisions criminalizing sexual activity between consenting adults in 2014 and 2016.15

Given the above evidence, I find that the Appellant has established, on a balance of probabilities, that his sexual identity has been exposed in Sierra Leone. And, based upon the objective evidence, there is no state protection or IFA for the Appellant in Sierra Leone. I find that he faces more than a mere possibility of persecution, if he were to return and therefore, his appeal is allowed.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. This appeal is allowed.
